its pronoun

classical

Sen. Ep. 124.16: cum ad initium ejus admōtus est
Traupman 335

ejus

pronoun: genitive of is

its (of something else)

As for “his” and “her”: when the owner is not the subject. tamquam equus reminīscitur viae cum ad initium ejus admōtus est, the start of it, of the road.

Other words

  • suus, sua, suum — its (own), referring to the subject

    pronoun (possessive, reflexive), declension · classical · Cic. Sen. 52: claviculīs suīs quasi manibus; Mart. 4.32.2: apis nectare clūsa suō

    When the owner is the subject: the vine claviculīs suīs … complectitur, holds on with its tendrils. Gellius shows both in one sentence: the Gauls call the wind that blows ex suā terrā (their own land) after turbine ejus (its whirling).

Examples

  • tamquam equus reminīscitur viae cum ad initium ejus admōtus est

    as a horse remembers a road when it is brought to the start of itSen. Ep. 124.16

  • nostrī namque Gallī ventum ex suā terrā flantem, quem saevissimum patiuntur, circium appellant ā turbine, opīnor, ejus ac vertīgine

    For our Gauls call the wind that blows from their own land, which they find the fiercest, circius, from its whirling and turning, I think.Gell. 2.22.20

  • vītis quidem, quae nātūrā cadūca est et, nisi fulta est, fertur ad terram, eadem, ut sē ērigat, claviculīs suīs quasi manibus quicquid est nacta complectitur

    The vine, which by nature droops and falls to the ground unless it is propped, raises itself by clasping with its tendrils, as with hands, whatever it finds.Cic. Sen. 52

  • et latet et lūcet Phaethontide condita guttā, ut videātur apis nectare clūsa suō

    The bee lies hidden and shines, shut in a drop of amber, so that it seems enclosed in its own nectar.Mart. 4.32.1–2

See also it, his, her, their, itself.
